title: Pip’s Rocket Lab
tagline: Let some air out. Predict the push!
learningGoal: Predict the direction a balloon rocket or a rocket starts moving when gas escapes from its opening.
childTakeaway: Gas goes one way. The rocket gets pushed the other way.
story: Pip is trying a balloon on a string before imagining a space journey. Help Pip predict each launch, then use the same idea for a rocket.
introPip: Let’s try my balloon rocket! Air is a kind of gas. Watch: air goes out one way, and the balloon gets pushed the other way. Which way will it go next?
conceptImageAlt: Smiling silver-gray Pip watches a blue balloon taped to a straw on a string between two supports. Soft puffs leave the balloon’s right-hand opening. An inactive silver-and-blue rocket stands nearby in daylight.

ageSupport.entry: Before round one, a grown-up points to the opening and demonstrates air leaving one way while the balloon travels the other way. The child can point to the large blue circle or yellow triangle instead of naming left and right.
ageSupport.stretch: Round five applies the same opposite-direction push to a rocket starting from rest in space. It can be skipped without blocking the story’s finish.

misconception: A rocket needs nearby air or the ground to push against. Its push comes from expelling its own gas; the engine can also push a rocket in space.

rounds.title: Which way will the balloon go?
rounds.prompt: Air comes out toward the yellow triangle. Which marker will the balloon move toward?
rounds.sceneAlt: A teal balloon hangs from a straw on a level string. Its opening and air puffs face a yellow triangle on the right. A blue circle sits on the left.
rounds.success: Air leaves toward the triangle. That pushes the balloon the other way, toward the circle.
hints: Find the opening where the air comes out.
Watch a slow demonstration: the air leaves on one side while the balloon slides the other way.
The air goes toward the yellow triangle, so the balloon goes toward the blue circle.
rounds.visualHint: In a future demonstration, animate air leaving to the right and the balloon moving left together. Reveal two contrasting direction arrows only after the child asks for a hint.
rounds.whyThisRound: An easy first prediction follows the introductory demonstration and checks the opposite-direction relationship.

rounds.title: Turn the balloon around
rounds.prompt: Pip turned the balloon around. Air comes out toward the blue circle. Which marker will the balloon move toward?
rounds.sceneAlt: A green balloon hangs on the same level string. Its opening and air puffs are on the left, beside the blue circle. A yellow triangle remains on the right.
rounds.success: Turning the opening around changes the push. Air goes toward the circle, and the balloon moves toward the triangle.
hints: Look again at the opening. It changed sides.
Pretend one hand is escaping air. Move your other hand the opposite way.
Air goes toward the blue circle. The balloon goes the other way, toward the yellow triangle.
rounds.visualHint: Animate the reversed experiment with synchronized air and balloon motion. Keep the marker positions fixed so the changed opening is the meaningful difference.
rounds.whyThisRound: The changed example reveals whether the child uses the opening rather than repeating the last marker or following balloon color.

rounds.title: A balloon tied shut
rounds.prompt: This balloon is tied shut and held still. No air can escape. When Pip lets go, will it zoom along the string or stay here?
rounds.sceneAlt: An inflated teal balloon is attached to a straw on a level string. A large visible knot closes its neck. There are no air puffs. Blue-circle and yellow-triangle markers sit at opposite ends.
rounds.success: No air is escaping, so there is no rocket push. On our level string, the still balloon stays here.
hints: Find the knot. Is there an open place for the air to leave?
Compare it with the open balloon: the open one lets air out, but this one keeps air inside.
A tied balloon has no escaping air to give it a rocket push. This one stays where Pip left it.
rounds.visualHint: Show the tied balloon remaining still, then replay a separate open balloon releasing air and sliding. Avoid implying that all stationary rockets are out of fuel.
rounds.whyThisRound: Checks whether inflation alone is mistaken for propulsion. The question states no escaping air and no starting motion.

rounds.title: A rocket uses the same idea
rounds.prompt: This rocket starts still. Hot gas shoots down from its engine. Which way will the rocket start moving?
rounds.sceneAlt: An upright silver-and-blue rocket has a visible engine and a stylized hot-gas plume extending below it. A star sits above and a flower sits below, with no motion arrows.
rounds.success: The rocket pushes hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. It is the same opposite-direction idea as the balloon.
hints: Look at the engine opening. Which way is the gas going?
Use the balloon idea: gas goes one way, and the rocket gets pushed the other way.
Gas goes down, so this rocket gets pushed up toward the star.
rounds.visualHint: Slowly animate gas downward and rocket upward together. Keep the plume off the ground so it cannot be read as a spring pushing on a launchpad.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfers the mechanism from cold air in a balloon to hot gas in a rocket, while changing the direction to vertical.

rounds.title: Optional: the push works in space
rounds.prompt: This rocket is still in space. It sends gas toward the blue circle. Which way can it start moving?
rounds.sceneAlt: A sideways silver-and-blue rocket floats among sparse stars with no ground. Its engine and gas plume face the blue-circle marker on the left. A yellow-triangle marker is on the right.
rounds.success: Gas goes toward the circle, and the rocket gets pushed toward the triangle. Its own escaping gas gives the push, even in space.
hints: The rocket brings its own gas-making materials. It can push gas out here too.
Imagine the balloon turned this way. Where would it get pushed?
The gas goes toward the blue circle. The rocket starts moving the opposite way, toward the yellow triangle.
rounds.visualHint: Animate the rocket and its gas moving apart in otherwise empty space. Do not add surrounding air, a surface, or a trailing plume that touches another object.
rounds.whyThisRound: An optional stretch checks opposite-direction transfer without a ground or nearby air. This introduces space thrust rather than testing prior space knowledge.

finale: Pip launches the balloon toward its chosen marker, then imagines a rocket journey: gas out one way, Pip’s rocket off the other way.
offlineActivity: With a grown-up, thread a string through a straw and stretch the string level between two supports. The adult inflates a balloon, holds its neck closed, and tapes it to the straw. Point to where its air will escape, predict its travel, and release. Reverse the balloon and try again. The adult handles balloons and cleans up any broken pieces.
reviewQuestions: Do the blue-circle and yellow-triangle markers make direction easier to point at, or would two familiar destination objects be clearer?
Should the tied-balloon comparison remain round three, or would a second open-balloon prediction better fit the Gems lesson’s existing challenge level?
Should the space example stay as the optional fifth round, or be saved for a later rocket lesson after children have tried the physical balloon?
designNotes: This is an adult concept pack. Its wording, diagram recognition and 2–4 minute target have not been tested with children.
The static scenes show where gas escapes, not where the vehicle moves. No unassisted scene includes motion arrows or a highlighted answer.
A short movement demonstration before round one is required. Static diagrams alone cannot show the push mechanism.
Visible pale puffs stand in for invisible balloon air. They must be explained as a picture showing where air goes, not as smoke or a new material.
The string guides a balloon along one line. It is not an engine, and real rockets do not need strings.

Questions use vehicles starting from rest. The model simplifies friction, gravity and thrust strength; it does not imply that gas direction always equals an already-moving spacecraft’s overall travel direction.
The upright rocket is an illustrative launch with enough thrust to rise. No landing, orbit, countdown arithmetic, fuel chemistry or rocket safety lesson is included.
The generated story image has decorative proportions and a slightly angled string. The deterministic SVGs govern the level-string teaching comparison.
The fifth-round circle and triangle are screen direction markers, not physical objects or destinations floating in space.
Built-in image generation was used for concept.png. The five SVGs are deterministic diagrams.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education — Simple Rocket Science
sources.supports: A straw-and-string balloon experiment, prediction and repeat observation, opposite direction of escaping air and balloon motion, and reversal of the balloon opening.

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center — Rocket Thrust
sources.supports: Rocket engines expel hot gas and generate thrust in vacuum without surrounding air. Supports the optional space-transfer explanation.
